\section{Methods: risk aggregation and stress testing}
\label{sec:aggregation-stress}
% The numbers of this section are macros written by tables/make_aggregation-stress.py from data/derived/C18; the tables and the
% figures are generated by tables/make_aggregation-stress.py and figures/make_aggregation-stress.py.
\input{tables/aggregation-stress-numbers}

A bank holds capital against four risks that its models measure separately: credit risk, market risk, interest rate risk in the
banking book (IRRBB) and operational risk. Two questions follow, and supervisors pose both in the assessment of capital
adequacy. The first is aggregation: how the capital of the separate risks combines into one figure when the dependence between
the risks is not known. The second is stress testing: whether the capital that remains after the losses of an adverse
macroeconomic scenario still meets its requirements over a planning horizon of three years. This section describes the four
methods that the validation applies to these two questions, the cases that exercise them and the committed computations that
Section~\ref{sec:results-aggregation-stress} reads.

The governing framework is the second pillar of the Basel framework. The European Central Bank guide to the internal capital
adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) asks that risk quantification methodologies are adequate, consistent and independently
validated, that key parameters such as confidence levels and correlations are consistent across risk types, that a
stress-scenario approach to the economic perspective reaches a conservatism comparable to a 99.9 percent economic capital
concept, and that regular stress testing ensures capital adequacy in adverse circumstances; it adds that supervisors do not in principle recognise inter-risk
diversification in the supervisory review \citep{aggregation-stress:ecb2018}. The Basel Committee principles for stress testing
require that models and methodologies for scenario impacts are fit for purpose and that stress testing models, results and
frameworks are subject to challenge and regular review \citep{aggregation-stress:bcbs2018}, and the guidelines of the European
Banking Authority on institutions' stress testing define the sensitivity analysis, the scenario analysis and the reverse stress
test \citep{aggregation-stress:ebagl2018}. In Chile the same assessment is the self-assessment of effective equity (IAPE) of the
financial market commission (CMF): a three-year horizon, an internal effective equity target of at least 8 percent of the
risk-weighted assets plus the systemic, conservation and countercyclical buffers, the bank's own estimate of capital for risks
not covered by the first pillar and a voluntary buffer, and a summary table in its Annex~3 \citep{aggregation-stress:cmf2025}. The supervisory exercises supply the reference practice that the methods are
compared with: the 2025 EU-wide stress test holds the balance sheet static and lets banks apply their own satellite models under
constraints \citep{aggregation-stress:ebanote2025,aggregation-stress:ebaresults2025}, and the Federal Reserve publishes the
documentation of its supervisory credit-loss models together with the loss rates of hypothetical portfolios
\citep{lgd-ead:fedmethod2025,aggregation-stress:fedcredit2026}.

Two cases of the product cover this area. Case C18, the capital aggregation of the ICAAP and the IAPE under macroeconomic
scenarios, uses real macroeconomic paths (the Federal Reserve 2026 baseline and severely adverse scenarios
\citep{aggregation-stress:fedscen2026}, the EBA and ESRB 2025 adverse scenario \citep{aggregation-stress:ebanote2025} and the
Delayed transition scenario of the NGFS \citep{aggregation-stress:ngfs2024}) and a synthetic bank, Banco Andino, whose book and
capital are calibrated to public aggregates. Its satellites are fitted on 1985 (1991 for two loan types) to 2019 and validated out of time on 2020
onward. It asks how far the aggregate capital depends on the assumption about the dependence between the four risks, whether
satellites estimated before an episode reproduce that episode, and how far the capital ratio falls under each scenario. Case C19
is a known-answer case on the supervisory stress test models: the Federal Reserve publishes the loss rates of hypothetical
portfolios, and the question is whether an implementation of the published equations reproduces them. Money in this section is
in billions of Chilean pesos (CLP $10^{9}$), rates and ratios are shown in percent, and every simulated quantity carries the
Monte Carlo standard error that the artifact records.

The four methods are the aggregation of the four capitals under dependence uncertainty with the allocation of the result and its
model risk (Section~\ref{sec:m25}); the macro satellites that carry a scenario to losses and to the capital ratio
(Section~\ref{sec:m26}); the replication of the supervisory credit-loss models of the Federal Reserve
(Section~\ref{sec:m27}); and the vector autoregression and growth-at-risk quantile satellites, which are fitted beside the
regression satellites on the same data (Section~\ref{sec:m31}). Section~\ref{sec:results-aggregation-stress} reports the
results of the methods on the cases.

% method: capital aggregation
\subsection{Capital aggregation: the dependence band, the Euler allocation and model risk}
\label{sec:m25}

\paragraph{Theory.}
Let $L_k$ be the loss of risk $k=1,\dots,K$ over one year, with $K=4$ here (credit, market, IRRBB and operational risk), and let
$\mathrm{EL}_k=\E[L_k]$ be its expected loss. Capital is economic capital on the unexpected-loss basis, the value at risk at level
$q$ less the expected loss; the expected loss is additive, so the simple sum of the capitals equals the comonotonic capital of
the total. The first two rows of the band are the simple sum and the square-root rule
with an inter-risk correlation matrix $R$,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{EC}_k=\VaR_q(L_k)-\mathrm{EL}_k,\qquad
\mathrm{EC}^{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{EC}_k,\qquad
\mathrm{EC}^{\mathrm{vc}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{EC}^{\top}R\,\mathrm{EC}},
\label{eq:ag-ec}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{EC}$ is the vector of the $K$ capitals, $q=\agstLevel$ is the confidence level, and $R$ is symmetric positive
semidefinite with a unit diagonal. The square-root rule is exact for elliptical losses with a common quantile scaling and an
approximation otherwise. Neither row is a bound: the value at risk is not subadditive, so the simple sum is not an upper bound
of the capital of the total in general, and the comonotonic dependence is not the worst case
\citep{aggregation-stress:embrechts2002,aggregation-stress:embrechts2013}.

The copula rows separate the marginals from the dependence. By Sklar's theorem the joint distribution is
$F(x_1,\dots,x_K)=C\bigl(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_K(x_K)\bigr)$ for a copula $C$ and the marginal distribution functions $F_k$. The
aggregate is simulated by drawing $U\sim C$, mapping each component through its marginal quantile function and summing,
\begin{equation}
L_k=F_k^{-1}(U_k),\qquad L=\sum_{k=1}^{K}L_k,\qquad
\mathrm{capital}_{\mathrm{row}}=\VaR_q(L)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{EL}_k,\qquad
\mathrm{DF}_{\mathrm{row}}=\frac{\mathrm{capital}_{\mathrm{row}}}{\sum_{k}\mathrm{EC}_k},
\label{eq:ag-copula}
\end{equation}
where $F_k^{-1}$ is the marginal quantile function in money, $\mathrm{capital}_{\mathrm{row}}$ is the capital of a row of the
band, and $\mathrm{DF}_{\mathrm{row}}$ is its diversification factor against the simple sum. The Gaussian copula draws
$Z=Ae$ with $AA^{\top}=R$ and $e$ a vector of independent standard normal variables, and sets $U=\Phi(Z)$ with $\Phi$ the
standard normal distribution function. The Student $t$ copula with $\nu>2$ degrees of freedom draws $W=\nu/\chi^2_{\nu}$
independent of $Z$, sets $X=\sqrt{W}\,Z$ and $U=t_{\nu}(X)$, with $t_{\nu}$ the $t$ distribution function and $\chi^2_{\nu}$ a
chi-square variable \citep{credit-capital:li2000,credit-capital:freymcneil2003,credit-capital:demartamcneil2005}. For a singular
matrix such as the all-ones matrix of the comonotonic case the factor $A$ is the eigen factor with the null eigenvalues set to
zero. The two families share the Kendall rank correlation, and they differ in the tail,
\begin{equation}
\tau=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\rho,\qquad
\lambda_{t}=2\,t_{\nu+1}\!\left(-\sqrt{\frac{(\nu+1)(1-\rho)}{1+\rho}}\right),
\label{eq:ag-tail}
\end{equation}
where $\rho$ is an off-diagonal entry of $R$ and $\lambda_t$ is the coefficient of tail dependence of the $t$ copula; the
Gaussian copula has $\lambda=0$ for $\lvert\rho\rvert<1$ \citep{credit-capital:demartamcneil2005}.

The bounds on the value at risk of the total for any dependence come from the rearrangement algorithm of
\citet{aggregation-stress:embrechts2013}. For marginal quantile functions $F_j^{-1}$, $j=1,\dots,K$, a level $\alpha$ and $N$
cells, two $N\times K$ matrices of lower and upper cell values are built on the tail beyond $\alpha$,
\begin{equation}
\underline{x}_{ij}=F_j^{-1}\!\Bigl(\alpha+(1-\alpha)\tfrac{i-1}{N}\Bigr),\qquad
\overline{x}_{ij}=F_j^{-1}\!\Bigl(\alpha+(1-\alpha)\tfrac{i}{N}\Bigr),\qquad
s(X)=\min_i\sum_{j}x_{ij},
\label{eq:ag-cells}
\end{equation}
and every column is rearranged to be oppositely ordered to the sum of the others until the smallest row sum $s$ stops
increasing; the values $s(\underline{X}^{*})\le s(\overline{X}^{*})$ bracket the worst value at risk and converge to it as $N$
grows. The best value at risk, the lower bound, is obtained in the same way on $[0,\alpha]$ by minimising the largest row sum.
No distribution function is inverted, because the quantile functions are evaluated on the grid. The authors note that an
analytic proof of convergence for all initial configurations remains open and use a random permutation of the columns as the
mitigation \citep{aggregation-stress:embrechts2013}; an adaptive variant of the algorithm is introduced by
\citet{aggregation-stress:hofert2015}. Algorithm~\ref{alg:ag-rearrangement} states the procedure as the engine runs it.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Rearrangement bounds on the value at risk of the total (lower and upper ranges).}
\label{alg:ag-rearrangement}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require marginal quantile functions $F_1^{-1},\dots,F_K^{-1}$, level $\alpha$, cells $N$, accuracy $\varepsilon$, sweep limit, seed
\Ensure ranges $[t_N,\bar t_N]$ (best value at risk) and $[s_N,\bar s_N]$ (worst value at risk)
\State build $\underline{X}$ and $\overline{X}$ on $[\alpha,1)$ and $\underline{Z}$ and $\overline{Z}$ on $[0,\alpha]$ by Equation~\eqref{eq:ag-cells}
\For{each matrix $M$ and its objective (maximise the smallest row sum, or minimise the largest)}
  \State permute every column of $M$ at random under the seed
  \Repeat
    \For{$j=1,\dots,K$}
      \State sort column $j$ so that it is oppositely ordered to $\sum_{l\neq j}M_{\cdot l}$
    \EndFor
    \State evaluate the objective on the row sums
  \Until{the objective changes by less than $\varepsilon$ between two sweeps, or the sweep limit is reached}
\EndFor
\State \Return the two ranges and whether all four runs stopped on the accuracy
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The allocation of the aggregate capital to the risks uses the Euler principle. For a risk measure $\rho$ that is positively
homogeneous of degree one and differentiable, the Euler contributions $\rho(L_k\mid L)=\tfrac{d}{dh}\rho(L+hL_k)\vert_{h=0}$ add
up to the total and are the only ones compatible with the return on risk-adjusted capital \citep{credit-capital:tasche2008}.
The product allocates the expected shortfall, whose contributions are conditional expectations over the tail of the total, and
reports the Euler diversification benefit of each risk,
\begin{equation}
\ES_q(L_k\mid L)=\E\bigl[L_k\mid L\ge\VaR_q(L)\bigr],\qquad
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\ES_q(L_k\mid L)=\ES_q(L),\qquad
B_k=1-\frac{\ES_q(L_k\mid L)}{\ES_q(L_k)},
\label{eq:ag-euler}
\end{equation}
where $\ES_q$ is the expected shortfall at level $q$ and $B_k$ is the Euler benefit of risk $k$. The expected shortfall is chosen
over the value at risk because the contribution of the value at risk is conditioned on a single point and is very noisy in
simulation, the caveat that \citet{credit-capital:tasche2008} states; the shortfall is a coherent measure
\citep{credit-capital:acerbitasche2002}, and the sample estimator puts exactly the mass $1-q$ in the tail.

Model risk is measured on the band itself. With a reference model $X_0$ and a set of models whose largest and smallest value of
the risk measure are $\overline{\rho}$ and $\underline{\rho}$, the add-on and the relative measure of
\citet{aggregation-stress:barrieu2015} are
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{AM}=\frac{\overline{\rho}}{\rho(X_0)}-1,\qquad
\mathrm{RM}=\frac{\overline{\rho}-\rho(X_0)}{\overline{\rho}-\underline{\rho}}\in[0,1],\\
\sup_{m\ge 0,\ \E[m]=1,\ \E[m\log m]\le\eta}\E[mV],\quad m_\theta=\frac{e^{\theta V}}{\E[e^{\theta V}]},
\end{gathered}
\label{eq:ag-modelrisk}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{AM}+1$ is the multiplier that brings the reference to the worst case, the capitals of the band rows are the
risk measures, and the last expression is the worst expected loss over likelihood ratios $m$ within a relative-entropy budget
$\eta$ for a loss function $V$, solved by the exponential tilt $m_\theta$ with $\theta>0$ chosen so that the entropy equals
$\eta$ \citep{aggregation-stress:glasserman2014}. Both quantities are sensitivity information and never a capital requirement.

\paragraph{Assumptions.}
All marginals are taken at one horizon, one year, and one confidence level, $q=\agstLevel$, so a marginal read at another level
is converted by the caller; the marginals are inputs and carry their own estimation error, which the band does not propagate;
the dependence is summarised by the correlation matrix in the elliptical rows and is arbitrary in the bounds; and the
rearrangement bounds are numerical approximations for which convergence is not proved. A diversified row above the simple sum is
a true result for a measure that is not subadditive, so the product reports it and repairs nothing. The headline capital of the
case is the simple sum, because the supervisory practice recognises no inter-risk diversification
\citep{aggregation-stress:ecb2018}, and because the Joint Forum found aggregation models still in development and not generally
relied on by supervisors \citep{aggregation-stress:jointforum2010}; every other row is labelled information.

\paragraph{Parameters.}
The simulated rows use $\agstDraws$ draws in chunks of $\agstChunk$ rows under the seed $\agstSeed$, the same for every row so
that the band is reproducible. The correlation matrix, ordered as credit, market, IRRBB and operational risk, and its stressed
version with the market-credit entry raised to 0.8 are
\begin{equation}
R=\agstCorrMatrix,\qquad R^{\mathrm{stress}}=\agstCorrStressMatrix .
\label{eq:ag-corr}
\end{equation}
The entries are the benchmark of \citet{aggregation-stress:rosenberg2006}, market-credit 0.5 and market and credit with
operational 0.2; no source consulted gives an inter-risk correlation for IRRBB, which is therefore treated as a market-type risk
(0.5 with credit and market, 0.2 with operational) as a convention of the case that the band shows the effect of. The value
0.8 stands for a high market-credit correlation, the stress that the validation of an economic capital model calls for, and it is
an upper value, not a published one; the ranges compiled by \citet{aggregation-stress:kuritzkes2003} are the context
\citep{aggregation-stress:rosenberg2006}. The degrees of freedom of the $t$ copula are $\nu\in\{\agstNuSet\}$; the largest value
approaches the Gaussian copula and the validation asks for several values. The rearrangement bounds use $N=10^{5}$ cells and the
accuracy $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$. Each marginal commits its quantile function on a grid of $\agstGridPoints$ probabilities
$\Phi(z)$ for $z$ from $-\agstGridZ$ to $\agstGridZ$ in steps of $\agstGridStep$, which is dense where a quantile function bends
and reaches the first and last of the $10^{6}$ simulated losses. The marginals come from the other cases of the product: the
credit marginal is the grouped copula of the six segments of the credit capital case, with 400 representative names per segment
(the value at risk and the shortfall were also measured with 1,600 names, and the difference stays within two standard errors);
the market marginal is the mixed-portfolio value at risk and expected shortfall of the market case, moved from 99 percent and one
day to 99.9 percent and one year by the ratio of the normal quantiles of the two levels and the square root of 250 trading days
(two conventions), scaled to the market share of the risk-weighted assets on the assumption that the position value is the market
risk-weighted assets of Banco Andino, and represented by the zero-mean $t$ distribution that reproduces them; the IRRBB marginal
is the one-factor Hull-White simulation of the interest rate case; and the operational marginal is the aggregate loss
distribution of the operational risk case with the frequency scaled to the assets of the bank.

\paragraph{Complexity.}
A simulated row costs $O(SK^{2})$ operations for $S$ draws to apply the factor $A$, $O(SK\log G)$ to interpolate the $K$
quantile functions on a grid of $G$ points, and $O(S\log S)$ to sort the totals for the value at risk and the shortfall; the
$t$ family adds one chi-square draw per row. The draw itself needs $O(SK)$ memory ($32$ MB for $\agstDraws$ draws of four
risks, from the 320 MB the engine documentation gives for $10^{7}$). The rearrangement algorithm costs $O(KN\log N)$ per sweep,
because each sweep sorts $K$ columns of $N$ entries, and it is run four times for a band (two ranges, two matrices each); the
engine documentation reports about 1.6 s per level at eight marginals and $N=10^{5}$ on the development device.

\paragraph{Implementation.}
The band is the function \texttt{dependence\_band} of the module \texttt{riskvalidation.\allowbreak aggregation.\allowbreak band} of the engine
\texttt{riskvalidation} 1.1.0, which calls \texttt{aggregation.simple} (the sum, the square-root rule and the correlation check),
\texttt{aggregation.\allowbreak copulas.\allowbreak copula\_\allowbreak aggregate} (the Gaussian and $t$ rows), \texttt{aggregation.\allowbreak bounds.\allowbreak worst\_\allowbreak var\_\allowbreak bounds} (the
two bounds) and returns the whole band, never a scalar. The Euler contributions are \texttt{portfolio.\allowbreak euler.\allowbreak es\_\allowbreak contributions},
the model risk measures are in \texttt{aggregation.model\_risk}, and the tests are in \texttt{validation.aggregation}; the
interface is the contract \texttt{engine-aggregation-api}. The case maps the engine's result onto the document in
\texttt{data-pipeline/pipeline/cases/c18/aggregation.\allowbreak py}.

\paragraph{Comparison and acceptance.}
The band is compared with its own rows and with published references. The engine reproduces the printed values of the worst
value at risk of eight Pareto marginals of \citet{aggregation-stress:embrechts2013}: at 99 percent the comonotonic value is
72.00 and the worst value is 141.67 (the engine measures the range 141.663 to 141.669), and at 99.9 percent the values are 244.98
and 465.29 (range 465.276 to 465.295). The capital of the marginals under normal marginals is compared with the square-root rule, which is exact there. The additive
overestimate of the simple sum is given beside the 30 to 40 percent that \citet{aggregation-stress:rosenberg2006} report for their
own bank, as context only: the range belongs to other marginals and weights, so it is not a test of the product and no light is
attached to it in the tables of this report. The acceptance criterion of the design document of the product is that the Euler contributions sum to the total and
that the band, with the simple sum, the square-root rule, the Gaussian and $t$ copulas and the worst case, is always shown. The
engine's tests attach a light to each comparison with a Contraste internal threshold, not a regulatory one,
\begin{equation}
\frac{\mathrm{capital}}{\mathrm{EC}^{\mathrm{vc}}},\qquad
\max_{\nu}\Bigl\lvert\frac{\mathrm{capital}_{t,\nu}}{\mathrm{capital}_{\mathrm{Ga}}}-1\Bigr\rvert,\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{capital}_{\mathrm{MC}}-\mathrm{EC}^{\mathrm{vc}}}{\mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{MC}}},
\label{eq:ag-tests}
\end{equation}
with the light red when the aggregate exceeds the simple sum, green for the copula-choice statistic up to 0.05 and amber up to
0.15, and green for the Monte Carlo agreement when the absolute statistic is at most 3; here $\mathrm{capital}_{t,\nu}$ and
$\mathrm{capital}_{\mathrm{Ga}}$ are the capitals of the $t$ and Gaussian rows and $\mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{MC}}$ is the Monte Carlo
standard error.

% method: macro satellites
\subsection{Macro satellites and the scenario chain to capital}
\label{sec:m26}

\paragraph{Theory.}
A macroeconomic stress test has three layers: a scenario generator for macro-financial variables, satellite models that map the
scenario variables to risk parameters, and a balance-sheet and capital engine that turns losses into capital ratios under a
balance-sheet assumption. The satellite of a segment default or loss rate
$\mathrm{DR}_{s,t}$ is the autoregressive distributed-lag form
\begin{equation}
g(\mathrm{DR}_{t})=\alpha+\sum_{k=1}^{p}\phi_k\,g(\mathrm{DR}_{t-k})+\sum_{l=0}^{q}\beta_l^{\top}X_{t-l}+\varepsilon_t,
\label{eq:st-ardl}
\end{equation}
where $g$ is a link function (probit $\Phi^{-1}$, logit or identity), $\alpha$ is the intercept, $\phi_k$ are the autoregressive
coefficients of order $p$, $X_t$ is the vector of macroeconomic regressors with distributed-lag coefficients $\beta_l$ up to lag
$q$, and $\varepsilon_t$ is the error. The form is generic in the family of macroeconomic credit risk models of
\citet{aggregation-stress:wilson1998} and \citet{aggregation-stress:virolainen2004}; it is not an equation of either paper. The
probit link is the choice consistent with the one-factor asymptotic model of \citet{ratings:gordy2003}: with asset
correlation $\rho$, a through-the-cycle default probability $\bar p$ and a systematic factor $Z_t$, the conditional default
probability of a name is $\Phi\bigl((\Phi^{-1}(\bar p)-\sqrt{\rho}Z_t)/\sqrt{1-\rho}\bigr)$, and in a large portfolio the default
rate equals it, so that
\begin{equation}
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{DR}_t)=\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\bar p)-\sqrt{\rho}\,Z_t}{\sqrt{1-\rho}},
\label{eq:st-vasicek}
\end{equation}
which is a linear function of the latent credit cycle $Z_t$; regressing the probit of the rate on macroeconomic variables is
therefore a regression of the cycle on them. The identity link is the linear form of the Federal Reserve's own default
probability regression \citep{aggregation-stress:fedcredit2026}, and it is used for the segments whose rate is zero or negative in some quarters (net recoveries).

The coefficients are estimated by ordinary least squares on an explicit window, with the classical standard errors,
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta=\arg\min_{\beta}\lVert y-X\beta\rVert^{2},\qquad
s^{2}=\frac{\lVert y-X\hat\beta\rVert^{2}}{n-k},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{s^{2}\bigl[(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\bigr]_{jj}},
\label{eq:st-ols}
\end{equation}
where $y$ is the vector of link values, $X$ the design matrix with an intercept, the lags and the regressors, $n$ the number of
observations of the window after the largest lag and $k$ the number of coefficients. A scenario enters through its path.
A scenario published after the model's reporting date cannot be used as if it were known then, so the shape of the published
path, its change from its own jump-off, is transposed onto the last observed value of the same series, with the periods aligned
by their distance from the jump-off; an annual path is joined linearly to quarterly values,
\begin{equation}
x^{\mathrm{target}}_{k}=x^{\mathrm{target}}_{0}+\bigl(L_{k}-L_{0}\bigr),\qquad
x_{y,k}=x_{y-1}+(x_{y}-x_{y-1})\frac{k}{4},
\label{eq:st-transpose}
\end{equation}
where $L_k$ is the published level in period $k$ after the jump-off $L_0$, $x^{\mathrm{target}}_{0}$ is the last observed value,
and $x_{y,k}$ is quarter $k$ of year $y$ from the year-end levels $x_{y-1}$ and $x_y$. Past the published horizon the engine
reverts a path linearly to the baseline over a convention of twelve quarters. The projected rates of the five loan types are
mapped to the loan classes of Banco Andino with fixed weights and turned into the loss of each year and into the capital path,
\begin{equation}
\ell_y=\sum_{c}E_c\,\bar r_{c,y}+\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{mkt}}+\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{op}},\qquad
\mathrm{CET1}_y=\mathrm{CET1}_0-\sum_{j\le y}\ell_j,\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{CET1}_y}{\mathrm{RWA}},
\label{eq:st-capital}
\end{equation}
where $E_c$ is the exposure of class $c$, $\bar r_{c,y}=\sum_{s}w_{c,s}\cdot\tfrac14\sum_{t\in y}\hat r_{s,t}$ is the mean of the
four quarterly annualised rates of year $y$ of the loan types $s$ that class $c$ maps from with weights $w_{c,s}$, $\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{mkt}}$
and $\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{op}}$ are the annual expected losses of the market and operational marginals, and $\mathrm{RWA}$ is constant on the static balance
sheet. IRRBB enters no loss: a change of economic value is not a profit-and-loss item of the banking book, and the rate path acts
on the net interest income, which the loss-only path does not credit. The market and operational terms are unstressed expected
losses, because no source maps a macroeconomic path to them, so the scenario loss is a floor on the loss of the stress. The
loss-only path credits no revenue: it is a depletion, not a forecast of capital, and the ratios it ends at depend on these
choices.

\paragraph{Assumptions.}
The satellites are statistical associations estimated on a stated window, and a projection under a scenario is scenario
analysis, not a forecast. They are fitted on United States charge-off rates and applied to Banco Andino through a fixed class
map, a labelled adaptation. Only series of agencies are read as regressors. The balance sheet is static, following the EBA
rules that maturing exposures are replaced by similar instruments, that stage~3 exposures are not cured and that no capital
measure is taken after the reference date \citep{aggregation-stress:ebanote2025}. The standard errors are classical, without
correction for heteroskedasticity or autocorrelation, so with an autoregressive term and overlapping data they are optimistic.

\paragraph{Parameters.}
The satellites use $p=\agstSatArOrder$ autoregressive lag, contemporaneous and one-quarter-lagged real GDP growth and
unemployment rate as regressors, and the fit window ending at \agstSatFitEnd. The commercial real estate and residential
satellites use the identity link and start in the first quarter of 1991, because the Board's table lacks both series before that
quarter and holds {\agstNonPosCre} and {\agstNonPosRes} quarters of non-positive rates in the window; the other three use the
probit link from the first quarter of 1985. The class map weights commercial and industrial and commercial real estate by 0.6
and 0.4 into the commercial class, credit cards and other consumer by 0.5 each into the consumer class, and takes residential
alone for the mortgage class. The expected signs are fixed before the fit: the autoregressive coefficient positive, the
growth coefficients negative, the contemporaneous unemployment coefficient positive and no sign claimed for its lag, which enters
as the offset of the first. The window length, the regressor set and the weights are choices of the case that the sources do not
fix; the engine hard-codes no sample end.

\paragraph{Complexity.}
A fit costs $O(nk^{2})$ for the normal equations with $k=6$ coefficients and $n\le\agstSatNMax$ observations, and a projection
over twelve quarters costs $O(12\,k)$ per loan type, so the whole chain of four scenarios and five loan types is negligible
against the aggregation simulation. The back-cast and the severity tests are $O(n)$. Algorithm~\ref{alg:st-chain} states the chain as
the case runs it.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{From a macroeconomic scenario to the loss path and the capital ratio of the static balance sheet.}
\label{alg:st-chain}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require quarterly history of the charge-off rates $\mathrm{DR}_s$ and of the regressors $X$, fit window $[t_0,t_1]$, links $g_s$, a scenario with published levels $L_k$ and jump-off $L_0$, the baseline tail, exposures $E_c$ and weights $w_{c,s}$, $\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{mkt}}$, $\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{op}}$, $\mathrm{CET1}_0$ and $\mathrm{RWA}$
\Ensure losses $\ell_y$ and CET1 ratios $\mathrm{CET1}_y/\mathrm{RWA}$ for the three years
\For{each loan type $s$}
  \State \textbf{if} the window reaches the episode that the satellite will be back-cast on \textbf{then} refuse the fit
  \State fit \cref{eq:st-ardl} by ordinary least squares on $[t_0,t_1]$ (\cref{eq:st-ols}) and record the estimates, the classical standard errors and the sign check against the declared signs
\EndFor
\State transpose the published level of each regressor onto its last observed value (\cref{eq:st-transpose}), join annual values linearly to quarters, and revert the path linearly to the baseline tail over twelve quarters after the published horizon
\For{each loan type $s$ and each projected quarter $t=1,\dots,12$}
  \State $\hat g_t\gets\alpha+\sum_k\phi_k\hat g_{t-k}+\sum_l\beta_l^{\top}X_{t-l}$, with the last observed link values and regressors before the jump-off; $\hat r_{s,t}\gets g_s^{-1}(\hat g_t)$
\EndFor
\For{each year $y=1,2,3$}
  \State $\bar r_{c,y}\gets\sum_sw_{c,s}\cdot\tfrac14\sum_{t\in y}\hat r_{s,t}$ for each class $c$, and $\ell_y\gets\sum_cE_c\bar r_{c,y}+\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{mkt}}+\mathrm{EL}^{\mathrm{op}}$
  \State $\mathrm{CET1}_y\gets\mathrm{CET1}_{y-1}-\ell_y$
\EndFor
\State \Return $(\ell_y)$ and $(\mathrm{CET1}_y/\mathrm{RWA})$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Implementation.}
The satellites are \texttt{riskvalidation.stress.satellites} (\texttt{fit\_satellite}, \texttt{project\_scenario},
\texttt{link} and \texttt{inverse\_link}) of the engine 1.1.0, the path handling is \texttt{stress.paths} (transposition,
annual to quarterly, reversion), the capital arithmetic is \texttt{stress.capital}, and the tests are in
\texttt{validation.stress}; the interface is the contract \texttt{engine-stress-api}. The case reads the sources and builds the
document in \texttt{data-pipeline/pipeline/cases/c18/satellites.py} and \texttt{scenarios.py}.

\paragraph{Comparison and acceptance.}
The satellites are compared with the realised charge-off rates of an episode that the fit never read. For an episode with
predicted rates $\hat y_t$ and realised rates $y_t$ the engine returns
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum_t(\hat y_t-y_t)^{2}},\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{peak}}=\frac{\max_t\hat y_t}{\max_t y_t},\\
\Delta=\arg\max_t\hat y_t-\arg\max_t y_t,
\end{gathered}
\label{eq:st-backcast}
\end{equation}
where $\rho_{\mathrm{peak}}$ is the ratio of the predicted to the realised peak and $\Delta$ is the timing error of the peak in
quarters. The light is green when the size deviation $\lvert\rho_{\mathrm{peak}}-1\rvert$ is at most {\agstPeakAmber} and the
timing error at most {\agstTimingQuarters} quarters, amber up to a size deviation of {\agstPeakRed}, and red otherwise; the test
refuses a fit window that reaches the episode. The scenario severity is the ratio of the peak deviation of a scenario variable
from its jump-off to the same deviation in the 2008 to 2009 crisis, with the light amber below {\agstSevMin}. The sign test
counts the coefficients whose estimate has the sign opposite to the declared one. The acceptance criterion of the design document of the product is that
satellites estimated on prior data back-cast through 2008 to 2009 and through 2020 and that the coefficient signs are checked.
The committed satellites of the baseline are fitted to the fourth quarter of 2019 and back-cast through 2020 to 2025; the 2008 to
2009 episode is back-cast by the regression satellite refitted to the fourth quarter of 2007, inside the comparison of
Section~\ref{sec:m31}.

% method: supervisory replication
\subsection{Replication of the Federal Reserve supervisory credit-loss models}
\label{sec:m27}

\paragraph{Theory.}
The Federal Reserve documents the credit-loss models of its supervisory stress test by portfolio type: corporate, commercial real
estate, first-lien mortgage, home equity, credit card, auto and other retail \citep{aggregation-stress:fedcredit2026}. Every
model multiplies a probability of default, a loss given default and an exposure at default for each facility and projection
quarter. The corporate model of the 2026 documentation is the template of the replication. Its expected loss, its default
probability regression and its loss rate are
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{EL}_{i,t}=\mathrm{PD}_{i,t}\,\mathrm{LGD}_{i,t}\,\mathrm{EAD}_{i},\qquad
\mathrm{LR}_{p}=\frac{\sum_{i,t}\mathrm{EL}_{i,t}}{\sum_{i}\mathrm{OB}_{i}},\\
\mathrm{vPD}_{r,n,t}=\alpha_{r,n}+\beta_{r,n}\,\mathrm{BBB}_t+\gamma_{r,n}\,\mathrm{BBB}_{t-4}+\varepsilon,
\end{gathered}
\label{eq:fed-el}
\end{equation}
where $i$ is a facility, $t$ a projection quarter, $\mathrm{vPD}_{r,n,t}$ is the quarterly average one-year vendor default
probability (divided by four) of rating group $r$ in industry group $n$, $\mathrm{BBB}_t$ is the BBB spread, the difference
between the BBB corporate yield and the ten-year Treasury yield, $\mathrm{BBB}_{t-4}$ is its four-quarter lag, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are
the coefficients of one of sixteen separate least squares regressions estimated on 2006 to 2023, and $\mathrm{LR}_p$ is the loss
rate of portfolio $p$, the cumulative nine-quarter loss divided by the sum of the initial utilised balances $\mathrm{OB}_i$. The
projected default probability applies the same equation with a lower bound of 0.25 basis points. The loss given default is one
minus a recovery rate that depends on collateral, lien and facility type and on the BBB spread at default, and the exposure at
default adds a constant 50 percent loan equivalent of the undrawn commitment to the outstanding balance,
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{LGD}_{i,t}=1-\bigl(a+b_{k(i)}+c\,\mathrm{Revolver}_i+d\,\mathrm{BBB}_t\bigr),\\
\mathrm{EAD}_i=\mathrm{OB}_i+\mathrm{LEQ}\,(\mathrm{CB}_i-\mathrm{OB}_i),
\end{gathered}
\label{eq:fed-lgd}
\end{equation}
where $a$ is the intercept, $b_{k(i)}$ is the effect of the collateral category $k(i)$, $c$ the effect of a revolving facility,
$d$ the coefficient of the BBB spread, $\mathrm{CB}_i$ the committed balance and $\mathrm{LEQ}$ the loan equivalent; the
documentation prints the intercept 0.750, the unsecured effect $-0.169$ and the BBB coefficient $-0.040$, and it bounds the loss
given default to the interval from zero to one. The other types follow the same decomposition with their own structures: a logit default probability and a
structural loss given default from collateral value for commercial real estate, ten transition equations for first-lien
mortgages, and hazard logits by account status and horizon for credit cards.

\paragraph{Assumptions.}
Three sets of assumptions bound a replication. The model and the scenario must be those of the answer key: the published loss
rates of the 2025 methodology belong to the 2024 severely adverse scenario over the nine quarters from the first quarter of 2024
and to portfolio data of the end of 2023, whereas the only public coefficients are those of the 2026 documentation
\citep{lgd-ead:fedmethod2025,aggregation-stress:fedcredit2026}. The 2025 corporate model projects the change of a
default probability that starts from a long-run average of vendor expected default probabilities, and it prints no coefficient.
The inputs of the public portfolio files are limited to the balances, the rating, the lien, the facility type and a two-digit
industry code. The tolerance of a replication is a modelling choice of the case, to be fixed before the computation and
justified by the spread that the unobserved inputs cause.

\paragraph{Parameters.}
No parameter is estimated: every coefficient is the Federal Reserve's. For the corporate default probability the documentation
prints sixteen coefficient triples by rating group and industry group; as an example the manufacturing BBB regression has
$\alpha=-0.055$, $\beta=0.056$ and $\gamma=0.014$, and in manufacturing the slope on the spread rises from 0.027 for the
highest rating group to 0.510 for the B group. The ``CCC-C'' group is pooled with industry intercepts. The scenario inputs are the BBB corporate
yield, the ten-year Treasury yield and four lagged quarters of the spread. The values that the case would fix itself are the
tolerance and the mapping of the portfolio files to the model groups, in particular the industry group of the finance codes,
which the file's two-digit code does not determine.

\paragraph{Complexity.}
The loss-rate computation is linear in the number of facilities $N_f$ and projection quarters $Q$, $O(N_fQ)$; the portfolios
published have 200 loans each and the horizon has $Q=9$ quarters, so a portfolio needs $1\,800$ facility-quarters.
Estimating the coefficients is out of scope, because they are published.

\paragraph{Implementation.}
The replication is not part of the engine \texttt{riskvalidation} 1.1.0: the engine documentation states that the supervisory
replication of the Federal Reserve models is outside the package, the stress module holds the satellites, the capital engine, the
reverse stress and the scenario models, and the pipeline of the product has no module for C19. No result of this method is
therefore committed, and the case has no document under the derived data. Algorithm~\ref{alg:fed-loss} states the procedure of
the published corporate computation that a replication would follow.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Loss rate of a hypothetical corporate portfolio under the published equations.}
\label{alg:fed-loss}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require facilities $i$ with rating, industry group, lien, revolver flag, committed and outstanding balance; scenario path of the BBB spread with four lagged quarters; coefficient tables
\Ensure loss rate $\mathrm{LR}_p$ of the portfolio
\For{each facility $i$ and projection quarter $t=1,\dots,9$}
  \State select the coefficient triple of the rating group and the industry group of $i$ and compute $\mathrm{PD}_{i,t}$ from $\mathrm{BBB}_t$ and $\mathrm{BBB}_{t-4}$, with the lower bound
  \State compute $\mathrm{LGD}_{i,t}$ from the collateral category, the revolver flag and $\mathrm{BBB}_t$, bounded to $[0,1]$
  \State compute $\mathrm{EAD}_i$ from the balances and the loan equivalent
  \State set $\mathrm{EL}_{i,t}=\mathrm{PD}_{i,t}\,\mathrm{LGD}_{i,t}\,\mathrm{EAD}_i$
\EndFor
\State \Return $\sum_{i,t}\mathrm{EL}_{i,t}\big/\sum_i\mathrm{OB}_i$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Comparison and acceptance.}
The comparison is with the published answer: the loss rates of the lower-risk, typical and higher-risk portfolios of each type,
printed in Tables 22, 27, 32 and 37 of the 2025 methodology and collected in Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-fedkey}. The
acceptance criterion of the design document of the product is that the published loss rates are reproduced within the tolerance
stated in the case,
\begin{equation}
\bigl\lvert\mathrm{LR}^{\mathrm{model}}_{p}-\mathrm{LR}^{\mathrm{published}}_{p}\bigr\rvert\le\delta\qquad\text{for every portfolio }p,
\label{eq:fed-accept}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{LR}^{\mathrm{model}}_{p}$ is the computed loss rate of portfolio $p$, $\mathrm{LR}^{\mathrm{published}}_{p}$ is the
printed one and $\delta$ is the tolerance of the case. This criterion is not met: no replication is run, so no
loss rate is compared with a tolerance and none is fixed, and the method stays open. The public files lack inputs that the models
require for all four types (Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-fedkey}), so none is replicable to its published loss rate from
them alone, and the report states no replication result.

% method: VAR conditional forecasts and growth-at-risk quantile satellites
\subsection{Vector autoregression conditional forecasts and growth-at-risk quantile satellites}
\label{sec:m31}

\paragraph{Theory.}
A vector autoregression (VAR) of order $p$ for $n$ variables is
\begin{equation}
y_t=c+\sum_{l=1}^{p}A_l\,y_{t-l}+u_t,\qquad u_t\sim(0,\Sigma),\qquad
\hat\Sigma=\frac{U^{\top}U}{T-p-(np+1)},
\label{eq:var-model}
\end{equation}
where $y_t$ is the vector of the variables, $c$ the intercept, $A_l$ the coefficient matrices, $u_t$ the shock with covariance
$\Sigma$, $U$ the matrix of the residuals of the equation-by-equation least squares fit, and $T$ the number of observations.
Bayesian versions shrink the coefficients toward a random walk \citep{aggregation-stress:litterman1986} and forecast well when
the system is large \citep{aggregation-stress:banbura2010}; global versions link country models through trade weights
\citep{aggregation-stress:pesaran2004,aggregation-stress:dees2007}. A stress scenario is a conditional forecast: the variables in
a set $c$ follow a given path and the free variables $f$ respond. With $\hat y_t=c+\sum_l A_ly_{t-l}$ the unconditional
one-step prediction, the conditional mean of period $t$ is
\begin{equation}
y_{c,t}=\mathrm{path}_t,\qquad
u_{c,t}=y_{c,t}-\hat y_{c,t},\qquad
y_{f,t}=\hat y_{f,t}+\Sigma_{fc}\,\Sigma_{cc}^{-1}\,u_{c,t},
\label{eq:var-cond}
\end{equation}
where $\Sigma_{fc}$ and $\Sigma_{cc}$ are the blocks of $\Sigma$ for the free and the conditioned variables; with a diagonal
$\Sigma$ the free variables follow their own equations with the conditioned path substituted. The period-by-period form is a
conditional mean and states no forecast density. Conditioning on every macroeconomic path of a first-order system returns the
regression satellite itself: the coefficient $\Sigma_{fc}\Sigma_{cc}^{-1}$ is the regression of the free shock on the conditioned
shocks, and by partitioned regression the fitted value equals that of the regression of the loss rate on its lag and on the
contemporaneous and lagged macroeconomic variables, which is the satellite of Section~\ref{sec:m26}. The maximum gap
between the two over every fit of the case is {\agstGapToOls} (the engine's check), so a VAR conditioned that way adds no model beyond the satellite, and the case
conditions on the realised GDP growth path alone while unemployment and the loss rate respond through the system.

Growth-at-risk replaces the mean with the distribution of future growth. Step one of \citet{aggregation-stress:abg2019} is a set
of quantile regressions of the growth $y_{t+h}$ over the next $h$ quarters on a vector $x_t$ of current
conditions, and step two fits a skewed $t$ density to the estimated quantiles,
\begin{equation}
y_{t+h}=\frac1h\sum_{j=1}^{h}g_{t+j},
\label{eq:gar-target}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta_\tau=\arg\min_{\beta}\sum_t\bigl[\tau\,\mathbb{1}(y_{t+h}\ge x_t\beta)+(1-\tau)\,\mathbb{1}(y_{t+h}<x_t\beta)\bigr]\lvert y_{t+h}-x_t\beta\rvert,\qquad
\hat Q_{y_{t+h}\mid x_t}(\tau)=x_t\hat\beta_\tau,
\label{eq:gar-quantile}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
f(y;\mu,\sigma,\alpha,\nu)=\frac{2}{\sigma}\,t\!\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma};\nu\right)T\!\left(\alpha\,\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\nu+1}{\nu+\bigl(\tfrac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\bigr)^{2}}};\ \nu+1\right),
\label{eq:gar-skewt}
\end{equation}
where, in \cref{eq:gar-target}, $g_t$ is the annualised growth rate of real GDP of quarter $t$, so that the product's target $y_{t+h}$ is the arithmetic mean of
the $h$ quarterly annualised rates (\texttt{realised} in \texttt{stress\_\allowbreak rungs.\allowbreak py}), $\tau$ is the quantile level, $\beta$ the regression coefficient vector, $\hat Q$ the conditional quantile, $\mu,\sigma$ the
location and scale, $\alpha$ the skewness and $\nu$ the degrees of freedom of the skewed $t$ density, and $t(\cdot;\nu)$ and
$T(\cdot;\nu)$ the Student $t$ density and distribution function. The target of the original paper is the annualised average
growth between $t$ and $t+h$; the two definitions coincide when growth is constant and differ when it changes sign inside the window,
as it does in 2020, and the reading of 2020 under the paper's definition is not recomputed here. The authors' main finding is that the lower quantiles move
strongly with financial conditions while the upper quantiles are stable \citep{aggregation-stress:abg2019}. A panel quantile
satellite for bank outcomes is the alternative of \citet{aggregation-stress:covas2014}; neither it nor the Bayesian VAR is
implemented in the engine.

\paragraph{Assumptions.}
The VAR is a reduced-form association over the fit window and not a structural model. The quantile regressions assume that the
coefficients fixed at the end of the training span hold on the later origins. The growth-at-risk regressors are real GDP growth
and the spread of the ten-year Treasury yield over the prime rate, because the national financial conditions index of the
original paper is not one of the series of agencies the case reads; it is a named substitution and not the paper's variable.
The skewed $t$ fit has four free parameters for the quantiles it matches, so it is exact only when the target is a skewed $t$,
and the fit reports a failure instead of filling a value when the search overflows near a normal shape.

\paragraph{Parameters.}
The VAR has {\agstVarLags} lag, equal to the autoregressive order of the satellite, on three variables: real GDP growth, the
unemployment rate and the linked loss rate, fitted on {\agstVarNMinGfc} to {\agstVarNMaxGfc} observations for the 2008 episode
and {\agstVarNMinPan} to {\agstVarNMaxPan} for the 2020 episode. Growth-at-risk uses the horizon of {\agstGarHorizon} quarters
and the quantile levels {\agstGarTaus}, with the regressors {\agstGarRegressors}, on {\agstGarTrainGfc} training origins from
{\agstGarTrainFirstGfc} to {\agstGarTrainLastGfc} for the first episode and {\agstGarTrainPan} origins from {\agstGarTrainFirstPan}
to {\agstGarTrainLastPan} for the second. Quantiles that cross at an origin are sorted and counted. Two windows are back-cast,
the global financial crisis (fit to the fourth quarter of 2007, prediction from the first quarter of 2008 to the fourth of 2009)
and the pandemic window (fit to the fourth quarter of 2019, prediction from 2020 to 2025). Each fit reads the training span
only, and a window whose fit ends at or after its start is refused as a leakage. The lag order, the horizon and the quantile
levels are choices of the case; they include the 5, 25, 75 and 95 percent quantiles that the second step of the original
paper matches with the skewed $t$ \citep{aggregation-stress:abg2019}, and the median.

\paragraph{Complexity.}
The VAR is fitted equation by equation in $O(Tm^{2}n)$ operations with $m=np+1$ regressors per equation, and each conditional
forecast period costs $O(n^{3})$ for the block solve; the quantile regressions are solved by iteratively reweighted least squares
at $O(Tk^{2})$ per iteration for $k$ regressors, with at most 5000 iterations per level. The skewed $t$ fit searches two shape
parameters by Nelder-Mead from four starts, solving the location and the scale exactly for each shape. Algorithm~\ref{alg:var-cond}
states the conditional forecast.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Period-by-period VAR conditional forecast given a path for a subset of the variables.}
\label{alg:var-cond}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require fitted $(c,A_1,\dots,A_p,\hat\Sigma)$, the last $p$ observations, a path $\mathrm{path}_t$ for the conditioned indices, horizon $H$
\Ensure forecast $y_t$ for $t=1,\dots,H$
\For{$t=1,\dots,H$}
  \State $\hat y_t\gets c+\sum_{l=1}^{p}A_l\,y_{t-l}$
  \State $y_{c,t}\gets\mathrm{path}_t$ and $u_{c,t}\gets y_{c,t}-\hat y_{c,t}$
  \State $y_{f,t}\gets\hat y_{f,t}+\hat\Sigma_{fc}\hat\Sigma_{cc}^{-1}u_{c,t}$
\EndFor
\State \Return $y_1,\dots,y_H$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Implementation.}
The functions are \texttt{fit\_var}, \texttt{var\_\allowbreak conditional\_\allowbreak forecast}, \texttt{gar\_\allowbreak quantile\_\allowbreak regressions} and
\texttt{fit\_\allowbreak skewed\_\allowbreak t\_\allowbreak to\_\allowbreak quantiles} of \texttt{riskvalidation.\allowbreak stress.\allowbreak scenario\_\allowbreak models} in the engine 1.1.0, scored with
\texttt{validation.\allowbreak stress.\allowbreak satellite\_\allowbreak backcast} and \texttt{sensitivity\_\allowbreak monotonicity}; the quantile regressions read the optional
dependency \texttt{statsmodels}. The case calls them in
\texttt{data-pipeline/pipeline/cases/c18/stress\_\allowbreak rungs.\allowbreak py} and writes the two records of the models document,
\texttt{c18-var-conditional-forecast} and \texttt{c18-growth-at-risk}. Neither the VAR nor the growth-at-risk regression feeds the scenario losses or the capital path.

\paragraph{Comparison and acceptance.}
The VAR is compared with the regression satellite refitted on the same training span and scored on the same quarters, so every
loan type shows both on one split; the growth-at-risk quantiles are compared with the unconditional quantile of the training span
through the pinball loss, $\mathrm{pinball}_\tau=\tfrac1n\sum_t\rho_\tau(y_t-q_t)$ with $\rho_\tau(d)=\tau d$ for $d\ge 0$ and
$(\tau-1)d$ otherwise, and the ratio of the two. The acceptance criterion of the design document of the product is that the VAR and the growth-at-risk regression back-cast through 2008 to
2009 and 2020 on prior data beside the regression satellites, with the coefficient-sign checks. The results are reported
whether either improves on the satellite or not.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:results-aggregation-stress}

\paragraph{The dependence band.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-band} and Figure~\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-band} show the band of case C18 over the four
marginals. The headline capital, the simple sum, is {\agstBandSum} billion; the square-root rule gives {\agstBandVc}, the
Gaussian copula {\agstBandGauss} (Monte Carlo standard error {\agstSeGauss}), the $t$ copula {\agstBandTFour}, {\agstBandTEight}
and {\agstBandTThirty} for four, eight and thirty degrees of freedom, and the rearrangement bounds {\agstBandLower} below and
{\agstBandWorst} above, a bracket of {\agstBandWidth} billion. The worst case lies {\agstWorstOverSum} percent above the simple
sum, which shows that the simple sum is not an upper bound, as the theory states. The Gaussian copula reaches {\agstGaussShare}
percent of the simple sum, a diversification benefit of {\agstDivBenefit} percent. The $t$ copula with eight degrees of freedom
and the square-root rule differ by {\agstDiffTEightVc} billion, far below the standard error of {\agstSeTEight}: for these
marginals they agree, which is an agreement of two numbers and not a property of the rules. The table does not show the
uncertainty of the marginals themselves, which the band does not propagate; the value at risk of the credit marginal alone has a
standard error of {\agstCreditSe} billion. The copula choice moves the capital by {\agstCopRelFour} percent at four degrees of
freedom, {\agstCopRelEight} percent at eight and {\agstCopRelThirty} percent at thirty, so the statistic of the copula-choice test
is {\agstCopStat} percent and its light is amber. Raising the market-credit correlation to 0.8 raises the Gaussian capital to
{\agstStressGauss} billion, {\agstStressRise} percent more, and the square-root rule to {\agstStressVc}, {\agstStressRiseVc}
percent more, while the bounds do not move, because they hold for any dependence. The additive overestimate of the simple sum
over the Gaussian capital is {\agstRsOver} percent; \citet{aggregation-stress:rosenberg2006} report {\agstRsLow} to {\agstRsHigh} percent
for the marginals and weights of their bank, which is context and not a comparison on the same data. What follows is that no single diversified figure should be read as the capital:
the band says that the answer for these marginals lies between {\agstBandLower} and {\agstBandWorst} billion depending on the
dependence, and the headline remains the simple sum.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{aggregation-stress-band}
\caption{The dependence band of case C18 at one year and 99.9 percent. Panel (a) shows the economic capital of each row of the band in CLP billion with an interval of two Monte Carlo standard errors for the simulated rows and the capital of the same row under a market-credit correlation of 0.8 as a diamond; panel (b) shows the Student t capital against the degrees of freedom beside the Gaussian capital and its two-standard-error band.}
\label{fig:aggregation-stress-band}
\end{figure}

\input{tables/aggregation-stress-band}

\paragraph{The allocation and the model risk.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-euler} and Figure~\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-euler} allocate the expected shortfall of the
Gaussian aggregate, {\agstEsTotal} billion, to the four risks: credit {\agstContribCredit}, market {\agstContribMarket}, IRRBB
{\agstContribIrrbb} and operational {\agstContribOper} billion, which add to the total with a relative error of {\agstEulerErr}
against the tolerance {\agstEulerTol}. Operational risk has {\agstEcShareOper} percent of the stand-alone capital and
{\agstShareOper} percent of the allocated shortfall, because its severity has a heavy tail: its shortfall is {\agstEsOverEcOper}
times its capital, against {\agstEsOverEcCredit} for credit risk. Its Euler benefit is the largest, {\agstBenefitOper} percent,
against {\agstBenefitMarket} percent for market risk, and the benefit of the portfolio is {\agstEsBenefit} percent. The table does
not say that the allocation is stable: the contributions are conditional expectations over a tail of one thousand scenarios of
the million simulated, so their sampling error is larger than that of the capital. The model risk measures on the band, with the
Gaussian copula as reference, are the add-on {\agstAm} and the relative measure {\agstRm}, for a reference capital of
{\agstRhoRef} billion between the extremes {\agstRhoMin} and {\agstRhoMax}; the entropy-constrained worst case of the expected
loss with a budget of {\agstGxBudget} is {\agstGxWorst} billion against the baseline {\agstGxBase}, a ratio of {\agstGxRatio}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{aggregation-stress-euler}
\caption{The Euler allocation of the expected shortfall of the Gaussian copula aggregate of case C18. Panel (a) compares, for each risk, its share of the sum of stand-alone economic capitals, of the sum of stand-alone expected shortfalls and of the allocated shortfall; panel (b) shows the Euler diversification benefit of each risk in percent.}
\label{fig:aggregation-stress-euler}
\end{figure}

\input{tables/aggregation-stress-euler}

\paragraph{The validation battery.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-battery} lists the {\agstLightsTotal} tests applied to the aggregation and the stress chain:
{\agstLightsGreen} are green, {\agstLightsAmber} amber and {\agstLightsRed} red. The aggregation tests are green except the copula
choice and the correlation stress, which are amber; the Monte Carlo capital agrees with the square-root rule under normal
marginals, with a statistic of {\agstEllipticalZ} standard errors, so the simulator is consistent with the closed form where the
closed form is exact. The bracket test is green: every row lies inside the bounds, whose width is {\agstBracketRatio} times the largest row.
The red lights are the sign test, with {\agstWrongSigns} of the {\agstSignDeclared} coefficients with a declared sign carrying the opposite sign (the intercept and the
lagged unemployment term of each satellite declare none), and the five back-casts of 2020 to 2025. The amber light of the severity test is the GDP growth path of the Federal Reserve
scenario, at {\agstSevGdp} of the 2008 to 2009 deviation against the threshold of {\agstSevMin}, while the unemployment path
reaches {\agstSevUnemp}, a peak deviation of {\agstSevUnempPeak} points against {\agstSevUnempHist}. The table does not show how
far a red light is from its threshold; the statistic and the metric columns carry that.

\input{tables/aggregation-stress-battery}

\paragraph{The satellites and the back-cast of 2020 to 2025.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-satellites} gives the fit of the five satellites: from {\agstSatNMin} to {\agstSatNMax}
observations, a coefficient of determination between {\agstSatRMin} and {\agstSatRMax}, and a wrong sign for
{\agstWrongCi} coefficient for commercial and industrial loans, {\agstWrongCre} for commercial real estate, {\agstWrongRes} for
residential, {\agstWrongCards} for credit cards and {\agstWrongOther} for other consumer. The high coefficients of
determination come mostly from persistence: the autoregressive coefficient of the commercial and industrial satellite is
{\agstSatExampleAr} (standard error {\agstSatExampleArSe}), while its contemporaneous unemployment coefficient is
{\agstSatExampleU} ({\agstSatExampleUSe}). Figure~\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-backcast-2020} shows the back-cast. The satellites
over-predict the rise of 2020: the credit card satellite predicts a peak of {\agstPeakPredCards} percent against a realised peak of
{\agstPeakRealCards} percent, a ratio of {\agstPeakRatioCards}, and the commercial real estate satellite {\agstPeakRatioCre}; {\agstBackcastRed} of the {\agstBackcastTotal}
back-casts are red. For every loan type except commercial and industrial loans the realised peak of the window falls years after
the predicted one, so the timing errors are large; the figure shows that the satellites reproduce the direction of the rise and not its size, consistent with the failure mode of
satellites estimated on calm periods and of a year in which fiscal support decoupled unemployment from defaults, an explanation
the case does not test.

\paragraph{The vector autoregression and the 2008 episode.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-var} and Figures~\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-backcast-2008} and
\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-var-ratio} compare the two models. In the 2008 to 2009 crisis the regression satellite is closer to the
realised rates for {\agstOlsCloserGfc} of the {\agstVarLoanTypesGfc} loan types and the vector autoregression for
{\agstVarCloserGfc}; the ratio of the errors runs from {\agstRatioGfcOther} for other consumer loans to {\agstRatioGfcCards}
for credit cards. In the 2020 to 2025 window the vector autoregression is closer for {\agstVarCloserPan} of
{\agstVarLoanTypesPan}, with ratios from {\agstRatioPanCre} for commercial real estate to {\agstRatioPanOther} for other consumer loans. The peak of the VAR is closer to the realised peak in the second window (a ratio of {\agstPeakVarPanCards}
for credit cards against {\agstPeakOlsPanCards} for the regression) but remains far from one for residential loans ({\agstPeakVarPanRes}), whose
realised peak is {\agstPeakRealRes} percent. {\agstVarWrong} of the {\agstVarChecks} sign checks of the VAR are red, and in each
of those the offending coefficient is the lagged unemployment term; the check of the growth-at-risk regressions has
{\agstGarWrong} wrong signs in {\agstGarChecks}. The results do not show that the VAR is the better model: it wins in the window
that the regression satellite over-predicts and loses in the 2008 to 2009 crisis for most loan types, and the red sign checks
say that its coefficient structure is not supported. The conditioning on GDP growth alone is the design that keeps the VAR from being
the satellite itself, with the gap of {\agstGapToOls} when both paths are given.

\paragraph{Growth-at-risk.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-gar} and Figure~\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-gar} score the quantile regressions. In the
2008 to 2009 window the mean pinball ratio to the unconditional quantile is {\agstGarRatioGfc} over {\agstGarOriginsGfc} origins,
narrowly below one, and in the 2020 to 2025 window it is {\agstGarRatioPan} over {\agstGarOriginsPan} origins, so the regression
is worse than the unconditional quantile there. At the first origin of the crisis, {\agstGarFirstDateGfc}, the 5 percent quantile
is {\agstGarFirstQGfc} percent and the realised growth of the next four quarters is {\agstGarFirstRealGfc}, below it; at
{\agstGarFirstDatePan} the quantile is {\agstGarFirstQPan} and the realised growth {\agstGarFirstRealPan}, not below it. In the
crisis all {\agstGarHitsHighGfc} origins fall below every predicted quantile, so the regression did not foresee the collapse; in
the second window {\agstGarHitsLowPan} of {\agstGarOriginsPan} fall below the 5 percent quantile, and the rates of
{\agstGarRateUpperPan} and {\agstGarRateHighPan} at the 75 and 95 percent levels are close to nominal. The results do not
show significance: the origins overlap, because consecutive origins share three of four target quarters, so the effective number
of origins is smaller than the count, and five origins cannot distinguish the ratio of {\agstGarRatioGfc} from one. Crossing quantiles
occur at {\agstGarCrossGfc} origin in the first window and {\agstGarCrossPan} in the second. The skewed $t$ density fitted to the five
quantiles of the first origin fails in the first window, where the engine's search overflows near a normal shape and the fit
reports the failure instead of a value; in the second window it gives the location {\agstSkewMuPan}, the scale {\agstSkewSigmaPan}, the skewness
{\agstSkewAlphaPan} and {\agstSkewNuPan} degrees of freedom, at a quantile distance of {\agstSkewDistPan}.

\paragraph{The scenarios and the capital path.}
Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-scenarios} and Figure~\ref{fig:aggregation-stress-scenarios} carry the four scenarios through the
satellites to the capital path. The CET1 ratio starts at {\agstCetStart} percent, {\agstCetStartAmount} billion of the risk-weighted
assets of {\agstRwa} billion. After three years of the loss-only path it stands at {\agstCetEndBaseline} percent under the baseline,
{\agstCetEndNgfs} under Delayed transition, {\agstCetEndFed} under the Federal Reserve severely adverse scenario and
{\agstCetEndEba} under the EBA adverse scenario; the total losses are {\agstCumLossBaseline}, {\agstCumLossNgfs}, {\agstCumLossFed}
and {\agstCumLossEba} billion. The legal minimum stack that serves as the failure point of the reverse stress is {\agstCetStack}
percent, so the two severe scenarios end below it and the baseline and Delayed transition above it. The comparison is of a depletion
with no revenue and a static balance sheet; even the baseline falls by {\agstDepletionBaseline} points, and none of the figures is
a forecast of capital. The stressed credit loss rests on satellites that fail their own back-cast of 2020 to 2025 (the red lights
of the battery), and the market and operational losses are unstressed, so the losses are a floor and the ratios above are
indicative of the chain and not an estimate of the capital the scenarios would leave. The scenarios are not equally severe by the test of the 2008 to 2009 deviation: all {\agstSevTotalNgfs}
variables of Delayed transition are amber, as is {\agstSevAmberEba} of the {\agstSevTotalEba} of the EBA scenario and
{\agstSevAmberFed} of the {\agstSevTotalFed} of the Federal Reserve one. The peak unemployment deviation is {\agstUnempPeakEba}
points in the EBA scenario and {\agstUnempPeakFed} in the Federal Reserve scenario, so the EBA scenario is the more severe in
unemployment and in the loss of the second year ({\agstCreditLossYTwoEba} against {\agstCreditLossYTwoFed} billion of credit loss).

\end{figure}

\paragraph{Supervisory replication.}
Case C19 has no committed computation. Table~\ref{tab:aggregation-stress-fedkey} lists the published answer keys, the loss rates
of the lower-risk, typical and higher-risk portfolios of each type, and the inputs that the public files lack. The corporate
loss rates are {\agstFedCorpLow}, {\agstFedCorpTyp} and {\agstFedCorpHigh} percent; the commercial real estate typical rate is
{\agstFedCreTyp}; the first-lien mortgage rates run from {\agstFedMortLow} to {\agstFedMortHigh}; and the credit card typical and
higher rates are {\agstFedCardTyp} and {\agstFedCardHigh} percent. The table shows what a replication would be
compared with and why it cannot be completed from public files; it shows no replication result, and the acceptance criterion of
the method (Section~\ref{sec:m27}) is not met.
